Second, a fix: I brought a bounded anti-diffusive correction from flux-corrected transport into the replay, weighted towards the vertical. It restores the thermocline from 15.7 millimetres to between 5.3 and 4.0, against 5.0 in the reference, and it never leaves the range of the data. Third, a limit: when the lid is cooled, the cooled fluid sinks and creates motion that is not in the recording, and no local correction can replace missing motion. So a database belongs to a flow regime, not just to a case.
cards.ingat: Diagnosis (trade-off + outlet) · koreksi terbatas (15,7 → 5,3–4,0 mm, ref 5,0) · batas (gerak yang hilang) · database milik rezim.

follow.q: Which result do you find most important?
follow.a: That a database belongs to a flow regime: a cooled lid creates motion that is not in an adiabatic recording, and no local correction can supply it (Th hlm. 67, 73).

cards.q: Why did you choose this method, and not another one, e.g. a neural network or a reduced-order model?
cards.who: S25 Ulrich · S18 Mara (“why this network type”)
cards.buku: Projection methods (POD–Galerkin) need closure, and thin moving temperature gradients are hard to represent with a few global modes (Th hlm. 1). rCFD keeps the full spatial resolution and the solver's own transport (Th hlm. 1–2). Larger learned models would need many paired states and would not provide the same bounds by construction (Th hlm. 74). Unlimited anti-diffusion is ill-posed, therefore the limiter (Th hlm. 32).
cards.kita: I chose recurrence CFD because my problem is a thin, moving thermocline. Reduced-order models with a few global modes struggle with such sharp, moving gradients, and they need closure models for whatever the modes do not capture. rCFD keeps the full mesh resolution and uses the transport of the real solver, so it conserves heat by construction. A neural network that predicts the whole field would need many paired states and gives no guarantee of conservation or boundedness. For the correction I chose a flux-corrected-transport limiter because simply reversing diffusion is ill-posed and blows up. The limiter makes it safe.
cards.ingat: ROM: susah untuk gradien tipis + perlu closure. NN: butuh banyak data, tanpa jaminan konservasi. rCFD: resolusi penuh, konservatif. Limiter: anti-difusi aman.

follow.q: Why not proper orthogonal decomposition?
follow.a: Projection methods need closure for what the modes miss, and thin moving temperature gradients are hard to represent with a few global modes (Th hlm. 1).

cards.q: Why did your extended replay work better than the standard replay?
cards.who: analog T2 (“why did mLSTM work better than attention”)
cards.buku: The face exchange can only move heat from warm to cold, so once a thermocline is diffused no $f_{sd}$ can restore it (Th hlm. 12). The correction moves heat up the local gradient. The direction matters more than the strength: weighted towards the vertical it reduces the thickness from 15.7 mm to 5.3–4.0 mm for $s=0.40$–$0.50$, and the trace error at $f_{sd}=0.5$ from 1.46 K to 0.70, 0.64 and 0.59 K. The unweighted correction reaches the reference thickness only with spurious grid-scale oscillations (Th hlm. 72). Sharper thermocline → correct outlet temperature → correct heat loss (Th hlm. 66).
cards.kita: The standard replay has only one tool, face exchange, and that tool can only smooth. Once the thermocline is smeared, more or less smoothing cannot bring it back. The extended replay adds the opposite operation, a bounded transfer of heat up the gradient, but only across the thermocline, in the vertical direction. That is the key point: the direction matters more than the strength. Applied in all directions, the correction makes grid-scale ripples. Applied across the front, it sharpens it cleanly. And because the outlet sits just below the thermocline, a sharper front also means the right temperature at the outlet and therefore the right heat loss. So it fixes both the layering and the energy budget.
cards.ingat: Face exchange hanya menghaluskan. Koreksi = naik gradien, arah vertikal. Arah > kekuatan. Front tajam → suhu outlet benar → energi benar.

follow.q: Why does the direction matter more than the strength?
follow.a: Exchanges across lateral faces act along the thermocline and amplify ripples. Weighted to the vertical, the correction acts only across the front (Th hlm. 33, 72).

cards.q: How did your main parameters affect the results?
cards.who: analog T2 (“how did the sequence length affect the results”)
cards.buku: Q1: no single $f_{sd}$ is best. Mean-temperature error is lowest with little or no mixing (RMSE 1.07 K), stratification height best near $f_{sd}=0.5$ (0.068 mm). Cost grows with mixing: 0.8 to 4.7 min per replay vs 569 min (Th hlm. 72). Q2: working range $s=0.40$–$0.50$ (Th hlm. 72). Wall-cooled: working point $s\approx0.55$, just above the bound $s\le1/2$ (Th hlm. 72–73). The database covers 600 s, so the replay cannot run beyond 600 recorded seconds (Th hlm. 11).
cards.kita: Two parameters matter most. The mixing strength of the standard replay controls a trade-off: little mixing gives the best mean temperature, while a value around 0.5 gives the best height of the warm layer. You cannot have both, because more mixing pushes warm fluid down to the outlet. More mixing also costs more time. The correction strength has a narrow working range, between 0.4 and 0.5 in the adiabatic case. Below it, the front is not sharp enough; above it, the strict bound of the limiter no longer holds. About the length of the data: the database covers 600 seconds and the flow is not recurrent, so the replay cannot go beyond those 600 seconds.
cards.ingat: $f_{sd}$: trade-off panas vs ketinggian (tak ada nilai terbaik tunggal). $s$: rentang kerja 0,40–0,50. Data 600 s, tak bisa diperpanjang.

follow.q: Why does stronger mixing cost more computing time?
follow.a: Strong face exchange needs many sub-steps per replay step. The floor-fed standard replay at $f_{sd}=160$ took 581 min instead of about 9 min (Th hlm. 68).

cards.q: Theory: explain the face exchange and why it cannot restore a gradient.
cards.who: S19 (“look at your theory part”) · S7 (rumus rinci) · S6 Hochreiter
cards.buku: For a face between $c_0$ and $c_1$ with $T_{c_1}\ge T_{c_0}$: $\Delta_{\text{swap}}=f_{sd}\,V_{\text{flip}}\,\frac{T_{c_1}-T_{c_0}}2$, $V_{\text{flip}}=\min(V_{c_0},V_{c_1})$, subtracted from the warm cell and added to the cold one. Conservative, and always from warm to cold (Th hlm. 12, Eq. 2.11). One replay step: $\mathbf T^{n+1}=\mathcal B(\mathcal C(\mathcal S(M^{(f_n)}\mathbf T^n)))$ (Th hlm. 12, Eq. 2.10).
cards.turunan:
1. Equal volumes $V$: the warm cell becomes $T_1-\frac{f_{sd}}2(T_1-T_0)$, the cold cell $T_0+\frac{f_{sd}}2(T_1-T_0)$.
  2. New difference: $T_1'-T_0'=(T_1-T_0)-f_{sd}(T_1-T_0)=(1-f_{sd})(T_1-T_0)$.
  3. The total $V(T_1+T_0)$ does not change: conservative.
  4. For $0<f_{sd}\le1$ the factor $1-f_{sd}$ lies in $[0,1)$: the difference can only shrink, never grow. So face exchange cannot sharpen a front, whatever $f_{sd}$ is. [Di luar skrip: langkah 1–4 adalah penurunan dari Eq. 2.11 untuk satu pertukaran; library membagi $f_{sd}$ ke beberapa sweep dengan batas per sweep]
cards.kita: Face exchange is how the replay adds mixing. At every internal face it moves a fraction of the temperature difference from the warmer cell to the colder one. If you write it out for two equal cells, the new difference is one minus $f_{sd}$ times the old difference, and the sum stays the same. So it is conservative, but the factor is always below one. It can only reduce differences. That is why no choice of the mixing strength can rebuild a thermocline that has been smeared: you need an operation that goes the other way.
cards.ingat: Selisih baru $=(1-f_{sd})\times$ selisih lama → hanya bisa mengecil. Konservatif.

follow.q: Why is the face exchange needed at all?
follow.a: A recorded displacement moves cell contents without mixing them. Molecular diffusion and sub-grid motion are not in the recording, so without the exchange the field would stay artificially sharp (Th hlm. 12).

cards.q: Theory: why is anti-diffusion dangerous, and how does your limiter make it safe? Is it conservative?
cards.buku: Heat equation $\partial_tT=D\,\partial_y^2T$: a Fourier mode decays as $\exp(-Dk^2t)$. With $D<0$ every mode grows as $\exp(|D|k^2t)$, the shortest fastest: ill-posed. On a model front, $\nu=-0.1$ amplifies a 1 mK disturbance by $1+4|\nu|=1.4$ per step and leaves the data range by more than 1 K after 21 steps (Th hlm. 31–32, Fig. 4.2). Limiter after Zalesak (1979): local bounds $T^{\min}_i,T^{\max}_i$ over the cell and its face neighbours; admissible energies $Q^+_h=C_h(T^{\max}_h-T_h)$, $Q^-_c=C_c(T_c-T^{\min}_c)$; exchange $\Delta q_f=s\min(Q^+_h,Q^-_c)$ from cold to warm (Th hlm. 32–33, Eq. 4.20–4.22). Bound $s\sum_fw_f\le1$: $s\le1/6$ unweighted, $s\le1/2$ vertically weighted (Eq. 4.23). Conservation: $\sum_iC_i\Delta T_i=\sum_f(\Delta q_f-\Delta q_f)=0$ (Eq. 4.18).
cards.turunan:
1. Insert $T=a(t)e^{iky}$ into the heat equation: $\dot a=-Dk^2a$, so $a(t)=a(0)e^{-Dk^2t}$. For $D<0$ the exponent is positive and grows with $k^2$: the finest ripples explode first.
  2. Discrete version: $T_j\leftarrow T_j+\nu(T_{j+1}-2T_j+T_{j-1})$. For the shortest mode $T_j=(-1)^j\varepsilon$, the bracket is $-4T_j$, so $T_j\leftarrow(1-4\nu)T_j=(1+4|\nu|)T_j$ for $\nu<0$. With $\nu=-0.1$: factor 1.4 per step.
  3. Limiter: a cell $i$ receives or gives at most $s\,Q_i\sum_{f\ni i}w_f$ in total. To stay inside $[T^{\min}_i,T^{\max}_i]$ we need $s\sum_fw_f\le1$.
  4. Unweighted, six faces with $w_f=1$: $s\le1/6$. Vertical weight: $\sum_fw^{\text{dir}}_f=2(\hat n_x^2+\hat n_y^2+\hat n_z^2)=2$, so $s\le1/2$. The direction weight triples the safe range.
  5. Every face moves $+\Delta q_f$ into one cell and $-\Delta q_f$ out of the other, so the total energy is unchanged.
cards.kita: Reversing diffusion means running the heat equation backwards, which is ill-posed: every Fourier mode grows, and the shortest ripples grow fastest. On a model front, even a disturbance of one millikelvin leaves the data range within about twenty steps. So I borrowed the idea of flux-corrected transport. For each cell I take the minimum and maximum of its neighbourhood, and across each face I move heat from the cold to the warm side, but only a fraction $s$ of what both cells can still take or give without crossing those bounds. Each face moves the same amount out of one cell and into the other, so energy is conserved exactly, and no new extremes appear. With the vertical weighting the bound guarantees this for $s$ up to one half.
cards.ingat: Anti-difusi: mode $e^{|D|k^2t}$, riak terhalus meledak. Limiter: $\Delta q=s\min(Q^+,Q^-)$, tak ada ekstrem baru, konservatif, aman sampai $s\le\frac12$ (vertikal).

follow.q: What happens above the bound $s\le1/2$?
follow.a: The bounds are no longer guaranteed by construction, and a final clamp may become active, removing energy that the conservation constraint then restores (Th hlm. 33, 69).

cards.q: Is your flow recurrent? Why can you call it rCFD then?
cards.buku: Recurrence matrix $R_{fg}=\|\Phi^{(f)}-\Phi^{(g)}\|$ (Th hlm. 9, Eq. 2.5). The matrix splits into two blocks at frame 315, when the warm inflow stops. Median recurrence prominence 0.028 and 0.027, about half the recommended lower limit 0.05; only 4.0% and 3.7% of vectors reach it (Th hlm. 10). The replay follows the 600 frames in order; it is rCFD in the data-based sense: recorded transport operators are replayed instead of solving the flow (Th hlm. 11).
cards.kita: No, my flow is not recurrent. The recurrence matrix splits into two blocks at second 315, when the warm inflow stops, and the recurrence prominence is about half of the recommended minimum. So I do not jump between similar frames. The replay goes through the 600 recorded frames in order. It is still recurrence CFD in the data-based sense: I replay stored transport operators instead of solving the flow again. The saving comes from skipping the momentum and pressure equations, not from extending the recording in time.
cards.ingat: Tidak rekuren: dua blok di frame 315, prominence 0,028 (< 0,05). Replay berurutan, tetap rCFD berbasis data.

follow.q: Could the replay run longer than the recording?
follow.a: No. Both recordings are non-recurrent, so the replay re-transports the 600 recorded seconds once and does not extrapolate in time (Th hlm. 11, 71).

cards.q: How much faster is it, and what does it cost?
cards.buku: Adiabatic reference 569 min; standard replay 2.16 min, extended 1.9 min: speed-ups about 260 and 300. Vessel: 8.5 and 8.6 min vs 7.4 and 4.7 days, about 1,250 and 790. Storage 2.4 GiB: the method exchanges storage for computing time. Face exchange takes almost half of the replay time, the conservation constraint almost a third (Th hlm. 68). The speed-up excludes the cost of generating the database, which equals one reference simulation (Th hlm. 71).
cards.kita: In the closed case the reference simulation needed 569 minutes and the extended replay about 1.9, so roughly 300 times faster. In the laboratory vessel it was about 800 to 1,250 times. The price is storage, 2.4 gigabytes for one database, and of course the one reference simulation needed to record it. So the method pays off when one recording is replayed many times, for example to compare operating conditions.
cards.ingat: 569 min → 1,9 min ≈ 300×. Vessel ≈ 790–1250×. Biaya: 2,4 GiB + satu simulasi rekaman.

follow.q: Where does the replay spend its time?
follow.a: Face exchange takes almost half of the loop and the conservation constraint almost a third, not the transport itself (Th hlm. 68).

cards.q: What are realistic applications? How would you use it in the real world?
cards.buku: Thermal storage, a steel ladle, a chemical reactor; a digital twin that updates a thermal model with plant data must keep pace with the process (Th hlm. 1). rCFD has been aligned with live plant data in vacuum treatment of steel (Zhang et al. 2025, Th hlm. 2). In the vessel, nudging to the rig thermocouples kept the replay cost at 9 to 11 min (Th hlm. 68).
cards.kita: Anywhere a thermal process must be simulated quickly and often: stratified hot-water storage, a steel ladle, a chemical reactor. The most interesting use is a digital twin, a model that runs next to the real process and is corrected with plant data. In my laboratory vessel case I already nudged the replay towards the measured thermocouple temperatures, and the replay still took only about ten minutes. That is the direction: fast physics-based replay plus measurements.
cards.ingat: Penyimpanan panas, ladle baja, reaktor, digital twin. Nudging ke sensor: tetap  10 menit.

follow.q: What does nudging do, and is it a prediction?
follow.a: The replay is pulled towards the measured temperatures at every step. Because it uses the measurements, it shows what the model adds to the data, not how well it predicts the rig (Th hlm. 68).

cards.q: What are the limitations? Are there issues with your data?
cards.buku: The reference is a simulation, so all agreement is with a simulation, not experimental validation. The fluid combines water and air properties ($Pr\approx42$), one mesh, no discretisation-uncertainty study: the selected strengths are results for this case, not general settings (Th hlm. 70). Databases are non-recurrent; the speed-up excludes the recording (Th hlm. 71). Vessel: settings chosen with each reference, single mesh, stirrer omitted, fields decoded from rendered frames, nudged runs are not predictions (Th hlm. 71). The replay cannot create motion absent from the database (Th hlm. 73).
cards.kita: I would name four. First, my reference is itself a simulation, so I show agreement with a simulation, not validation against an experiment. Second, I used one mesh and one fluid, whose thermal properties come from the solver's default for air, so the correction strengths I found belong to this case and are not general settings. Third, I chose the parameters with the reference available, so these are in-sample results, not predictions. And fourth, the fundamental one: the replay can never create motion that is not in the recording, such as the plume of a floor feed replayed with a lid-fed database.
cards.ingat: Acuan = simulasi · satu mesh, satu fluida ($Pr\approx42$) · parameter dipilih dengan acuan (in-sample) · tidak bisa membuat gerak baru.

follow.q: Why did you not validate against an experiment?
follow.a: There are no measurements for the closed configuration. I report agreement with a laminar simulation at $Re\approx100$; high-fidelity buoyant-jet measurements would be the next benchmark (Th hlm. 70).

cards.q: What would you do differently in hindsight? How could you extend the work?
cards.who: S14 Küng · S18, S20 Mara · S31
cards.buku: Future work (Th hlm. 73–74): let the recorded diffusivity act (shorter step or implicit exchange); apply the conservation constraint per compartment; record only the kinematic part $\rho c_p\mathbf v$ of the flux so it can transfer; switch databases according to the flow state; determine the correction strength from the flow state with a small network inside the limiter; test against measurements and on a second mesh.
cards.kita: In hindsight I would plan the validation from the start: a second mesh and a comparison with measurements of a buoyant jet, so the working strengths are not tied to one grid. I would also record the flux without the reference temperature, only its kinematic part, so that it can be transferred to other cases. As extensions, two things excite me most. First, switching between databases according to the current temperature field, so that a cooled lid or a floor feed gets the right motion. Second, letting a small neural network predict the local correction strength from the replayed field, inside the limiter, so that it stays conservative and bounded.
cards.ingat: Dari awal: mesh kedua + eksperimen. Rekam fluks kinematik. Lanjutan: ganti database sesuai keadaan + jaringan kecil untuk $s$ di dalam limiter.

follow.q: Why a small network and not a large one?
follow.a: A small network that predicts only the local correction strength acts inside the limiter, so conservation and the bounds still hold, and it needs far fewer training states (Th hlm. 74).

cards.q: Which work influenced your thesis the most? How does it connect to your studies?
cards.buku: Record-and-replay and the face exchange: Lichtenegger and Pirker (2016), Pirker and Lichtenegger (2018) (Th hlm. 8, 12). The limiter: flux-corrected transport, Boris and Book (1973), Zalesak (1979) (Th hlm. 3, 32–33). Selecting the next operator: method of analogues, a nearest-neighbour search (Th hlm. 8).
cards.kita: Two lines of work. The method itself comes from Lichtenegger and Pirker, especially their 2018 paper, which introduced the face exchange I analysed. The correction comes from a much older idea, flux-corrected transport by Boris and Book and the multidimensional limiter of Zalesak from 1979. From my studies, three courses meet here. Numerical methods in fluid mechanics, because the whole problem is numerical diffusion. Machine learning, because the method is data-based: it stores operators and finds the next one by a nearest-neighbour search, and I selected parameters against a reference much like hyperparameters on validation data. And the limiter works like a guardrail, a hard constraint that keeps the output inside the range of the data.
cards.ingat: Pirker & Lichtenegger 2018 (metode) + Zalesak 1979 (limiter). Kuliah: metode numerik, ML (nearest neighbour, pemilihan parameter), constraint.

follow.q: How does your limiter differ from Zalesak's?
follow.a: I use Zalesak's local bounds expressed as energies, but instead of scaling all exchanges of a cell together, I apply a fixed fraction $s$ of the smaller admissible amount at each face (Th hlm. 33).

title: Hoedt: optimisasi orde dua (bab yang ia tulis)

cards.q: Gradient descent is a first-order method. What does “second order” add?
cards.buku:
Every gradient descent step optimises a first-order Taylor approximation $	ilde R(\mathbf w+\Delta\mathbf w)=R(\mathbf w)+
abla R(\mathbf w)\Delta\mathbf w$ with a regularisation term that keeps the update small (Eq. 14.1). A second-order approximation adds the Hessian: $	ilde R(\mathbf w+\Delta\mathbf w)=R(\mathbf w)+
abla R\,\Delta\mathbf w+ rac12\Delta\mathbf w^T
abla^2R\,\Delta\mathbf w$ (Eq. 14.2). Curvature information is expensive but often gives much better updates that converge faster (D2 hlm. 341). The Hessian $H_{ij}=\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j$ is symmetric; if it is positive definite at a point, that point is a local minimum. For $P$ parameters it needs $O(P^2)$ memory (D2 hlm. 344, Eq. 14.8).
cards.turunan:
1. Minimise the linear model plus a penalty: $\min_{\Delta\mathbf w}\ \nabla R\,\Delta\mathbf w+\lambda\|\Delta\mathbf w\|^2$.
  2. Derivative zero: $\nabla R^T+2\lambda\Delta\mathbf w=0$, so $\Delta\mathbf w=-\frac1{2\lambda}\nabla R$. This is gradient descent with $\eta=\frac1{2\lambda}$ (D2 hlm. 341).
  3. So the learning rate is really a guess of how far the linear model can be trusted. Second-order methods replace this guess by the curvature.
cards.kita: Gradient descent only uses the slope. You can show that each gradient step minimises a linear approximation of the loss plus a penalty on the step size, and the learning rate is just that penalty. Second-order methods also use the curvature, the Hessian, so they know whether the valley is narrow or wide in each direction. That usually gives much better steps and faster convergence. The price is the size of the Hessian: for $P$ parameters it has $P$ squared entries, which is impossible to store for a network with millions of weights. So in deep learning we use approximations.
cards.ingat: GD = minimisasi model linear + penalti langkah (eta = 1 per 2 lambda). Orde dua = pakai kelengkungan (Hessian), tapi memorinya P kuadrat.

follow.q: Why is the learning rate like a trust parameter?
follow.a: Gradient descent minimizes the linear model plus $\lambda\|\Delta\mathbf w\|^2$, giving $\eta=1/(2\lambda)$. A large $\eta$ means we trust the linear model far away (D2 hlm. 341).

cards.q: Derive Newton's method. Why is it not used directly for deep networks?
cards.buku: Second-order Taylor approximation around $\mathbf w_{\text{ref}}$; its derivative is linear: $\partial\tilde R/\partial\mathbf w=J(\mathbf w_{\text{ref}})+H(\mathbf w_{\text{ref}})(\mathbf w-\mathbf w_{\text{ref}})$ (Eq. 14.11). Setting it to zero gives $\mathbf w^*=\mathbf w_{\text{ref}}-H^{-1}J$, the Newton direction $-H^{-1}\mathbf g$ (Eq. 14.12). On a quadratic error surface the Newton direction points directly to the minimum, one step finds it (Fig. 14.1). It needs a starting point close enough to the optimum (D2 hlm. 346–347). Full Hessian: $O(P^2)$ memory, inversion $O(P^3)$ (hlm. 344–345).
cards.turunan:
1. Newton finds a root of a function. A minimum is a root of the gradient, $\mathbf g(\mathbf w)=0$.
  2. Linearise the gradient: $\mathbf g(\mathbf w)\approx\mathbf g(\mathbf w_{\text{ref}})+H(\mathbf w-\mathbf w_{\text{ref}})$.
  3. Set to zero and solve: $\mathbf w^*=\mathbf w_{\text{ref}}-H^{-1}\mathbf g(\mathbf w_{\text{ref}})$.
  4. One dimension: $w^*=w-R'(w)/R''(w)$. The step is large where the curve is flat and small where it is steep. Quickprop (B5) is exactly this, with $R''$ estimated from two gradients.
  5. Check on $R(w)=\frac12cw^2$: $w-cw/c=0$, the minimum in one step, for any $c$. Gradient descent instead needs $\eta<2/c$ (A11).
cards.kita: Newton's method looks for a point where the gradient is zero. I take the second-order Taylor expansion of the loss, so the gradient becomes linear in the weights, set it to zero and solve. The update is minus the inverse Hessian times the gradient. On a quadratic bowl this jumps to the minimum in a single step, whatever the curvature, because it divides by the curvature automatically. For deep networks it is not used directly for three reasons: the Hessian has P squared entries, inverting it costs P cubed, and far from the minimum, or at a saddle point, the Hessian is not positive definite, so the Newton step can even go uphill.
cards.ingat: Newton: w baru = w dikurangi invers Hessian kali gradien. Kuadratik: satu langkah. Masalah: memori P kuadrat, invers P pangkat tiga, Hessian tak selalu definit positif.

follow.q: Why does Newton converge in one step on a quadratic?
follow.a: The second-order Taylor model is then exact, so the point where its gradient is zero is the true minimum (D2 Fig. 14.1).

cards.q: Line search versus trust region. What is the Armijo condition?
cards.buku:
Line search: choose a downhill direction, then find a step along it, ideally $\min_\eta R(\mathbf w+\eta\Delta\mathbf w)$ (Eq. 14.3). In practice trial and error, e.g. Armijo backtracking: start with $\eta_0$ and multiply by $ho\in(0,1)$ until $R(\mathbf w+\eta\Delta\mathbf w)\le R(\mathbf w)+c_1\eta
abla R\,\Delta\mathbf w$ (Alg. 14.1). Wolfe adds the curvature condition (D2 hlm. 342–343). Trust region: minimise a local model only inside a region $T$ where it is trusted (Eq. 14.4). Linear model and a ball of radius $r$: $\Delta\mathbf w=- rac{r}{\|
abla R\|}
abla R$. Quadratic model: $(H+\lambda I)\Delta\mathbf w^*=-\mathbf g$ with $\lambda(r-\|\Delta\mathbf w^*\|)=0$ (Eq. 14.6–14.7, hlm. 343–344).
cards.turunan:
1. Linear model in a ball: $ abla R\,\Delta\mathbf w=\| abla R\|\|\Delta\mathbf w\|\cos heta$ is smallest for $\cos heta=-1$ and $\|\Delta\mathbf w\|=r$. So $\Delta\mathbf w=-r\, abla R/\| abla R\|$: gradient descent with $\eta=r/\| abla R\|$.
  2. Quadratic model with the constraint as a Lagrange term: minimise $\mathbf g\Delta\mathbf w+ rac12\Delta\mathbf w^TH\Delta\mathbf w+ rac\lambda2(\|\Delta\mathbf w\|^2-r^2)$. Derivative zero: $\mathbf g+H\Delta\mathbf w+\lambda\Delta\mathbf w=0$, so $(H+\lambda I)\Delta\mathbf w=-\mathbf g$.
  3. $\lambda=0$: the step lies inside the region, it is the Newton step. $\lambda>0$: the step sits on the border, and $\lambda I$ makes $H+\lambda I$ positive definite and shortens the step.
cards.kita: Both are ways to decide how far to move. Line search first picks a direction, for example the negative gradient or the Newton direction, and then searches along that line for a good step size. A simple version is backtracking with the Armijo condition: start with a large step and shrink it until the loss decreases by at least a fixed fraction of what the slope predicts. Trust region turns it around. It first fixes a radius in which a local model of the loss is trusted, and then finds the best step inside that radius. With a quadratic model this gives the Hessian plus lambda times the identity, which is Newton when the step fits inside the region and closer to gradient descent when it does not.
cards.ingat: Line search: arah dulu, lalu panjang langkah (Armijo: turun cukup). Trust region: radius dulu, lalu langkah terbaik di dalamnya: Hessian tambah lambda I.

follow.q: When is a trust region method preferable?
follow.a: When the local model is only valid nearby. Its radius is easier to interpret than the $\lambda$ of Levenberg–Marquardt (D2 hlm. 354).

cards.q: How can we approximate the Hessian? What are quasi-Newton methods and BFGS?
cards.buku: Diagonal approximation: only $O(P)$ storage, inversion in $O(P)$, computed with one extra forward and backward pass, but crude (D2 hlm. 344–345). Outer-product approximation $B_{k+1}=B_k+\mathbf h_k\mathbf h_k^T$ (Eq. 14.9), inverse updated directly with Sherman–Morrison (Eq. 14.10). Quasi-Newton methods estimate the (inverse) Hessian from gradients, using the secant condition $\mathbf g_{\text{new}}-\mathbf g_{\text{old}}=H(\mathbf w_{\text{new}}-\mathbf w_{\text{old}})$ (Eq. 14.13). SR1: rank-one update (Eq. 14.17). BFGS: rank-two update $B_{\text{new}}=B_{\text{old}}+\frac{\Delta\mathbf g\Delta\mathbf g^T}{\Delta\mathbf g^T\Delta\mathbf w}-\frac{B\Delta\mathbf w\Delta\mathbf w^TB}{\Delta\mathbf w^TB\Delta\mathbf w}$ (Eq. 14.20), keeps the estimate positive (semi-)definite, so it moves towards minima, not saddle points. Algorithm: Newton direction $\mathbf d=-G\mathbf g$, line search for $\eta$, update $G$ (Alg. 14.2, hlm. 346–348).
cards.turunan:
1. Secant condition: the gradient of the quadratic model is $\mathbf g(\mathbf w)\approx\mathbf g_{\text{old}}+H(\mathbf w-\mathbf w_{\text{old}})$. At $\mathbf w_{\text{new}}$: $\Delta\mathbf g=H\Delta\mathbf w$. Two gradients tell us how $H$ acts along the last step.
  2. SR1: try $B_{\text{new}}=B_{\text{old}}+\alpha\mathbf u\mathbf u^T$ and require $\Delta\mathbf g=B_{\text{new}}\Delta\mathbf w$. Then $\Delta\mathbf g-B_{\text{old}}\Delta\mathbf w=\alpha(\mathbf u^T\Delta\mathbf w)\mathbf u$, so take $\mathbf u=\Delta\mathbf g-B_{\text{old}}\Delta\mathbf w$ and $\alpha=1/(\mathbf u^T\Delta\mathbf w)$ (Eq. 14.15–14.16).
  3. BFGS uses two such terms with $\mathbf u=\Delta\mathbf g$ and $\mathbf v=B\Delta\mathbf w$, which gives Eq. 14.20.
cards.kita: Since the full Hessian is too big, we approximate it. The cheapest way is to keep only its diagonal, one curvature value per weight, which costs one extra backward pass but ignores how weights interact. Quasi-Newton methods are smarter: they never compute second derivatives. They look at how the gradient changed between two steps. If the loss were quadratic, the change in gradient would be the Hessian times the change in weights, which is the secant condition. BFGS uses this to update an estimate of the inverse Hessian with two rank-one corrections per step, and it keeps the estimate positive definite, so the steps always point downhill. Then it does a line search along that direction.
cards.ingat: Diagonal: murah, kasar. Quasi-Newton: Hessian ditaksir dari selisih gradien (syarat secant). BFGS: update rank dua, tetap definit positif, plus line search.

follow.q: Why should the Hessian estimate stay positive definite?
follow.a: Then $-G\mathbf g$ is a descent direction and the method moves towards minima rather than saddle points; BFGS has this property (D2 hlm. 348).

cards.q: What is the conjugate gradient method?
cards.buku: Vectors are conjugate w.r.t. a symmetric positive definite $A$ if $\mathbf x_i^TA\mathbf x_j=0$ for $i\ne j$, i.e. orthogonal after a change of coordinates (D2 hlm. 349, Fig. 14.2). $P$ conjugate directions form a basis, so any $\mathbf w^*$ is reached in exactly $P$ steps (Eq. 14.22). With $A=H$ the coefficients equal the optimal line-search step sizes (hlm. 350). New direction $\mathbf d_{\text{next}}=\beta\mathbf d-\mathbf g_{\text{new}}$ (Eq. 14.27). Hestenes–Stiefel, Polak–Ribière $\beta=\frac{\mathbf g_{\text{new}}^T\Delta\mathbf g}{\mathbf g_{\text{old}}^T\mathbf g_{\text{old}}}$, Fletcher–Reeves $\beta=\frac{\mathbf g_{\text{new}}^T\mathbf g_{\text{new}}}{\mathbf g_{\text{old}}^T\mathbf g_{\text{old}}}$ (Eq. 14.30–14.33). Polak–Ribière is the most stable (hlm. 351–352).
cards.turunan:
1. Require the new direction to be conjugate to the old one: $\mathbf d^TH(\beta\mathbf d-\mathbf g_{\text{new}})=0$, so $\beta=\dfrac{\mathbf d^TH\mathbf g_{\text{new}}}{\mathbf d^TH\mathbf d}$ (Eq. 14.28).
  2. Remove $H$ with the secant condition $\Delta\mathbf g=\eta H\mathbf d$: $\beta=\dfrac{\mathbf g_{\text{new}}^T\Delta\mathbf g}{\mathbf d^T\Delta\mathbf g}$ (Hestenes–Stiefel).
  3. After an exact line search the new gradient is orthogonal to the last direction (Fig. 14.3). Using this twice simplifies the denominator to $\mathbf g_{\text{old}}^T\mathbf g_{\text{old}}$ (Polak–Ribière), and once more the numerator to $\mathbf g_{\text{new}}^T\mathbf g_{\text{new}}$ (Fletcher–Reeves).
cards.kita: Steepest descent zig-zags in a long narrow valley, because each new direction partly undoes the previous one. Conjugate gradients avoid this: each new direction is a mix of the new negative gradient and the previous direction, chosen so that it is conjugate to the old one with respect to the Hessian. Then a step along the new direction does not spoil the minimisation already done along the old ones. On a quadratic with $P$ parameters it finishes in at most $P$ steps. The mixing factor beta can be computed from gradients only, for example with the Polak-Ribière formula, so we never need the Hessian itself.
cards.ingat: Arah baru = beta kali arah lama dikurangi gradien baru, saling konjugat terhadap Hessian. Tanpa zig-zag, kuadratik selesai dalam paling banyak P langkah. Beta dari gradien saja.

follow.q: Why conjugate and not simply orthogonal directions?
follow.a: Conjugate directions are orthogonal after the change of coordinates $H^{1/2}$. Then a step along a new direction does not undo the minimization along the old ones (D2 hlm. 349).

cards.q: Derive the Levenberg–Marquardt update.
cards.buku:
Least squares: $R(\mathbf w)= rac12\|\mathbf r\|^2$ with residuals $r_n=g(\mathbf x_n,\mathbf w)-y_n$ and Jacobian $J_{ij}=\partial r_i/\partial w_j$. Then $
abla R=J^T\mathbf r$ and $
abla^2R=J^TJ+\sum_jr_j
abla^2r_j$; the second term can often be ignored, e.g. near the optimum where $r_j\approx0$ (Eq. 14.34–14.35). Linearised residual plus regulariser: $\min_{\Delta\mathbf w} rac12\|\mathbf r+J\Delta\mathbf w\|^2+ rac\lambda2\|\Delta\mathbf w\|^2$, giving $(J^TJ+\lambda I)\Delta\mathbf w=-J^T\mathbf r$ (Eq. 14.37–14.38). $\lambda=0$: Newton (with $H\approx J^TJ$). Large $\lambda$: gradient descent with step $1/\lambda$. Decrease $\lambda$ when the residuals decrease, increase it otherwise. Same as the trust-region update $(H+\lambda I)\Delta\mathbf w=-
abla R$, “the grandfather of trust region methods” (D2 hlm. 353–354).
cards.turunan:
1. Gradient: $\partial R/\partial w_j=\sum_ir_i\,\partial r_i/\partial w_j$, so $\nabla R=J^T\mathbf r$.
  2. Linearise: $\mathbf r(\mathbf w+\Delta\mathbf w)\approx\mathbf r+J\Delta\mathbf w$. The objective $\frac12(\mathbf r+J\Delta\mathbf w)^T(\mathbf r+J\Delta\mathbf w)+\frac\lambda2\Delta\mathbf w^T\Delta\mathbf w$ has derivative $J^T(\mathbf r+J\Delta\mathbf w)+\lambda\Delta\mathbf w$.
  3. Set to zero: $(J^TJ+\lambda I)\Delta\mathbf w=-J^T\mathbf r$.
  4. Large $\lambda$: $\lambda\Delta\mathbf w\approx-J^T\mathbf r=-\nabla R$, so $\Delta\mathbf w\approx-\frac1\lambda\nabla R$.
cards.kita: Levenberg-Marquardt is for least-squares problems. The gradient of half the squared residuals is the Jacobian transposed times the residuals, and the Hessian is approximately the Jacobian transposed times the Jacobian, which needs no second derivatives. I linearise the residuals, add a penalty lambda on the step size, and set the derivative to zero. That gives J transposed J plus lambda times the identity, times the step, equals minus the gradient. With small lambda it is a Newton-type step, with large lambda it becomes a small gradient-descent step. Lambda is adapted: if the error goes down we trust the model more and reduce lambda, otherwise we increase it. It is the same equation as a trust-region method.
cards.ingat: J transpose J tambah lambda I, kali langkah, sama dengan minus J transpose r. Lambda kecil: Newton. Lambda besar: GD dengan langkah 1 per lambda. Sama dengan trust region.

follow.q: Why is Levenberg–Marquardt limited to least squares?
follow.a: It approximates the Hessian by $J^TJ$ from the Jacobian of the residuals, which exists only for a sum of squared residuals (D2 hlm. 353).

cards.q: What are natural gradients?
cards.turunan:
1. Steepest descent with a KL constraint: $\min_{\mathbf d}L(\mathbf w+\mathbf d)$ s.t. $D_{KL}=c$.
  2. Lagrangian with first-order $L$ and second-order KL: $L(\mathbf w)+\nabla L^T\mathbf d+\frac\lambda2\mathbf d^TI_F\mathbf d-\lambda c$.
  3. Derivative zero: $\nabla L+\lambda I_F\mathbf d=0$, so $\mathbf d=-\frac1\lambda I_F^{-1}\nabla L$.
  4. Compare: plain GD is the same derivation with $\|\mathbf d\|^2$ instead of $\mathbf d^TI_F\mathbf d$, i.e. $I_F$ replaced by the identity.
cards.kita: Ordinary gradient descent measures the size of a step in parameter space, with the Euclidean norm. But two parameter changes of the same size can change the model's distribution very differently: moving the mean of a wide Gaussian by four changes much less than moving the mean of a narrow one. The natural gradient measures the step by how much the distribution changes, with the KL divergence. For small steps the KL divergence is approximately a quadratic form with the Fisher information matrix. Minimising the loss under that constraint gives the inverse Fisher matrix times the gradient. So it is like Newton's method, with the Fisher information playing the role of the Hessian, and the result does not depend on how we parameterise the model.
cards.ingat: Natural gradient = invers Fisher kali gradien. Langkah diukur dengan KL di ruang distribusi, bukan jarak Euclid. Fisher = Hessian dari KL. Tak bergantung parameterisasi.

follow.q: Why is the natural gradient invariant to the parameterization?
follow.a: It measures the step by the change of the distribution (KL divergence), not by the change of the parameter values (D2 hlm. 355–357).
